Using canregtools for Population-Based Cancer Registry Analysis

canregtools

2026-11-16

Source: vignettes/using-canregtools.Rmd
using-canregtools.Rmd
library(canregtools)
data("canregs")
registry <- canregs[[1]]

What canregtools does

canregtools is organised around a practical population-based cancer registry workflow. It helps users move from registry files or data frames to standardised case records, age-grouped cancer counts, rates, data-quality indicators, and analysis-ready reports.

The package uses two main object types. A canreg object keeps the registry at the record level. An fbswicd object keeps the same registry after cases have been cleaned, grouped by age, classified by cancer site, and counted. The separation is useful in practice: users can keep the source records for audit and reclassification while using the summary object for routine indicators.

The case-level canreg object

A single canreg object contains a registry identifier and three core tables:

  • FBcases: incidence or first-primary case records;
  • SWcases: mortality records; and
  • POP: population denominators by year, sex, and age group.

The case tables retain variables such as dates, sex, ICD-10 codes, morphology, and basis of diagnosis. The population table contains the denominator rks. Several registries are stored as a named canregs collection.

The summary-level fbswicd object

An fbswicd object is designed for downstream indicators. Its main summary table is keyed by year, sex, cancer, and agegrp, and contains the required first-primary count fbs. Its pop table is keyed by year, sex, and agegrp, and contains the denominator rks.

The summary table can also contain mortality and quality counts such as sws, mv, dco, mvs, ub, sub, ids, and mult. When available, sitemorp stores site and morphology frequency vectors, and exclude stores records excluded during cleaning. Several summary objects are stored as a named fbswicds collection.

Step 1: import or construct a canreg object

Read the standard Excel layout

When registry data are stored in the package’s expected Excel layout, use read_canreg(). A single workbook returns one canreg; a directory or a vector of workbooks returns a named canregs collection. The workbook name is used as the registry identifier.

registry <- read_canreg("data/410100.xlsx", pop_type = "long")
registries <- read_canreg("data/registries", pop_type = "long")

For a wide population sheet, set pop_type = "wide" and provide the relevant population-column arguments when the source layout differs from the defaults.

Construct from data frames already in R

Use as_canreg() when the incidence, mortality, and population data have already been imported or prepared. Separate incidence and mortality tables are accepted directly:

registry <- as_canreg(
  inci = incidence_data,
  mort = mortality_data,
  pop = population_data,
  regicode = "410100"
)

If one raw case table contains both incidence and death dates, it can be passed as regi_data:

registry <- as_canreg(
  regi_data = raw_registry_data,
  pop = population_data,
  year = 2023,
  regicode = "410100"
)

For multiple registries, keep the identifier in a column and use regicode_var. The column must be present in the required input tables, and the result is split into one named canreg object per registry:

registries <- as_canreg(
  inci = incidence_data,
  mort = mortality_data,
  pop = population_data,
  regicode_var = "registry_id"
)

The constructors standardise dates and year/sex fields and attach the component classes FBcases, SWcases, and POP. Keep registry identifiers as character values so that leading zeros are not lost.

Step 2: manage registry data before counting

The cr_* functions are the data-management layer between import and analysis. They work with the package’s object structure, so users can select registries, filter rows, combine batches, and aggregate areas without first flattening the object into one large data frame.

Select registries with cr_select()

Use cr_select() when the question is “which registry objects should I keep?” It selects elements from a canregs or fbswicds collection. Conditions are evaluated separately for each element. Population-oriented aliases make it possible to select registries by the number or range of available population years:

selected <- cr_select(canregs, pop_n_years == 3)
selected <- cr_select(
  canregs,
  all(pop_years %in% as.character(2018:2022))
)

The index argument can also select by registry names, positions, or a logical vector. For example, cr_select(canregs, index = c("410103", "410307")) keeps only the named elements. For a summary collection, conditions can refer to summary indicators such as inci or mv.

Filter rows with cr_filter()

Use cr_filter() when the question is “which records or summary strata should I keep inside these objects?” The part argument controls the components to which the row filter is applied. For a canreg, common choices are "FBcases", "SWcases", and "POP"; for an fbswicd, they are "fbswicd", "sitemorp", "pop", and "exclude". Use part = "all" when the same condition should be applied wherever its variables are available.

male_cases <- cr_filter(registry, sex == "1", part = "FBcases")
one_year <- cr_filter(summary_object, year == "2021", part = "all")
without_totals <- cr_filter(
  summary_object,
  drop = "total",
  part = "fbswicd"
)

This is the key distinction: cr_select() chooses registry elements, whereas cr_filter() filters rows within the chosen object’s components. Filtering case records can return NULL when both incidence and mortality become empty, so check the result before continuing the workflow.

Clean and inspect the standard components with cr_clean()

cr_clean() prepares FBcases, SWcases, and POP for counting. It assigns years, sex values, age groups, and cancer classifications while preserving the canreg structure. It is useful when users want to inspect the cleaned record-level tables before creating counts. count_canreg() calls the same cleaning stage internally when the next goal is an fbswicd summary.

cleaned <- cr_clean(
  registry,
  age_breaks = c(0, 1, seq(5, 85, 5)),
  cancer_type = "big"
)
head(cleaned$FBcases)

Combine batches with cr_combine()

Use cr_combine() to append compatible batches that represent the same registries, such as separate data deliveries or time periods. It accepts a list of homogeneous canregs objects or a list of homogeneous fbswicds objects. It retains registries that occur in only one input and preserves optional components when they are available.

all_batches <- cr_combine(list(registries_2021, registries_2022))

The inputs must be named collections, and the collection names must agree with the regicode stored in each element. Use cr_combine() for row-appending; use cr_merge() when the intended result is an aggregated registry.

Aggregate with cr_merge()

Use cr_merge() to pool the elements of a canregs or fbswicds collection into one object. Case records are appended, while population strata are summed by year, sex, and age group. For summary objects, matching count columns are aggregated into one fbswicd object. The result records the source registry identifiers so that the pooled result remains traceable.

pooled_registry <- cr_merge(canregs)
pooled_summary <- cr_merge(count_canreg(canregs, cancer_type = "big"))

Rename and reframe registry collections

cr_rename() changes selected registry names and updates the top-level regicode inside each renamed element. It is useful when source file names are not suitable for presentation or when analysis-specific labels are needed.

renamed <- cr_rename(
  canregs,
  c("410103" = "REG_A", "410307" = "REG_B")
)

cr_reframe() groups registries into a new administrative or reporting level and merges the registries within each group. Available classification levels can be inspected with ls_vars("reframe"); typical choices include "province", "city", "area_type", and "region".

city_level <- cr_reframe(canregs, strat = "city")
province_level <- cr_reframe(
  count_canreg(canregs, cancer_type = "big"),
  strat = "province"
)

Choose the operation according to the data-management goal:

  • select registry elements with cr_select();
  • filter rows or cancer categories with cr_filter();
  • prepare components for counting with cr_clean();
  • append compatible batches with cr_combine();
  • pool registries by summing compatible strata with cr_merge();
  • change presentation identifiers with cr_rename(); and
  • regroup registries by an administrative or reporting level with cr_reframe().

Step 3: count cases and create an fbswicd object

The usual next step is count_canreg(). It cleans the case records, assigns age groups, classifies cancer sites, and combines incidence, mortality, and population information into an fbswicd object.

summary_object <- count_canreg(registry, cancer_type = "big")
names(summary_object)
#> [1] "regicode" "fbswicd"  "sitemorp" "pop"      "exclude"

The default age groups follow the package’s standard breaks. For a specific analysis, supply age_breaks explicitly. For example, the following creates three broad age groups:

summary_object <- count_canreg(
  registry,
  age_breaks = c(0, 15, 65),
  cancer_type = "big"
)

Use cancer_type = "big", "small", "gco", or "ci5" according to the classification needed by the analysis. The age grouping and cancer classification are part of the summary step, so document them alongside the results.

If summary tables have already been calculated outside the package, use as_fbswicd() to create the same object contract:

summary_object <- as_fbswicd(
  fbsw = summary_table,
  pop = population_summary,
  sitemorp = site_morphology_summary,
  exclude = excluded_records,
  regicode = "410100"
)

Here fbsw must contain year, sex, cancer, agegrp, and fbs; pop must contain year, sex, agegrp, and rks. Optional components are kept when supplied. For multiple registries, use regicode_var in the two required tables.

Step 4: calculate the indicators you need

Once the fbswicd object is available, the same object can be passed to the main analysis functions. For example, calculate age-standardized rates, quality indicators, and age-specific rates as follows:

asr <- create_asr(summary_object, year, sex, cancer)
quality <- create_quality(summary_object, cancer)
age_rate <- create_age_rate(summary_object)

head(asr)

#> 6 2021  0     106         128 18.6       11.5      11.4          17.1

create_asr() returns the crude rate and standardised rates, including the China 2000 and World 1985 standard populations by default. It can also return confidence intervals, variance, or population columns. create_quality() returns indicators such as mortality-to-incidence, morphologically verified, death-certificate-only, and unknown-primary proportions when the corresponding counts are available. create_age_rate() returns rates by age group.

For site and morphology summaries, use the sitemorp component produced by count_canreg():

site_morphology <- create_site_morp(summary_object)

The package also provides comparison functions for multi-registry outputs. For example, compare_rate() compares rate outputs and compare_mv() evaluates morphologically verified percentages using the comparison registries in the same stratum. These functions should be used only after checking that the registries use compatible years, age groups, cancer classifications, and population definitions.

The complete user workflow

From a user’s perspective, the normal sequence is:

  1. read an Excel workbook or prepare data frames;
  2. create one canreg object per registry;
  3. choose the age grouping and cancer classification;
  4. call count_canreg() to obtain fbswicd objects;
  5. calculate rates, quality indicators, age-specific results, and site or morphology summaries; and
  6. compare registries or pass the results to a report workflow.

The sample data illustrate the complete path:

data("canregs")
registry <- canregs[[1]]
summary_object <- count_canreg(registry, cancer_type = "big")
asr <- create_asr(summary_object, year, sex, cancer)

c(registry = class(registry)[1], summary = class(summary_object)[1])
#>  registry   summary 
#>  "canreg" "fbswicd"
head(asr[c("year", "sex", "cancer", "cr", "asr_cn2000", "asr_wld85")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   year  sex   cancer    cr asr_cn2000 asr_wld85
#>   <chr> <chr> <chr>  <dbl>      <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 2021  0     101     5.53       3.74      3.79
#> 2 2021  0     102     0.73       0.71      0.71
#> 3 2021  0     103     8.58       4.53      4.85
#> 4 2021  0     104    17.9       11.1      11.2 
#> 5 2021  0     105    34.3       20.6      20.2 
#> 6 2021  0     106    18.6       11.5      11.4

For an audit-oriented workflow, validate_canreg() and validate_fbswicd() are available as optional checks before or after the summary step. They return structured issue tables without modifying the input; they complement, rather than replace, review of the source data and analysis assumptions.

Overall and sex-specific summary rows

Summary and population tables may supply male/female rows, overall rows (sex = "0"), or both. Before calculating rates or quality indicators, create_asr(), create_quality(), and create_age_rate() retain an existing overall row once at each original stratum. A missing overall row is generated from the available sex-specific rows. This happens before years or other strata are combined, preventing double counting when only some strata already have overall rows. When male, female, and overall rows are all supplied, inconsistent count or population totals cause an error. If only one sex is available alongside a supplied overall row, the supplied overall is retained; the missing sex is not inferred. Overall-only tables remain overall-only.

Sparse summary tables and zero-case age groups

For each year/sex/cancer stratum present in a summary table, rate and quality functions interpret absent age rows as zero cases and complete them using the matching population ages. Population for zero-case ages remains in the overall denominator. This interpretation requires a complete population table for the intended analysis and treats the summary table as a sparse count table, not as an incomplete collection of unknown observations.

An explicitly supplied NA, non-finite, or negative summary count causes an error rather than becoming zero. Entirely absent years, sexes, or cancers are not invented. Missing population rows are never generated as zero; ASR output requires every declared age group to be covered. If missing case rows mean unknown rather than zero, resolve those omissions before calculation instead of using them as a sparse zero-case table.

Project registry dictionaries

Use a project directory to keep registry mappings and labels with the analysis:

options(canregtools.dict_dir = file.path("config", "canregtools"))
cr_map(c("410103" = "410100"), attr = "registry")
write_regicode(data.frame(
  regicode = "410103", cname = "项目登记处", ename = "Project registry",
  abbr_cn = "项目", abbr_en = "Project"
))
ls_dict("registry")
ls_dict("regicode")
ls_dict_files(with_info = TRUE)

cr_map() updates grouping attributes for cr_reframe(); write_regicode() updates multilingual labels used immediately by tidy_var(), add_labels(), and ls_vars("regicode"). Label columns must be character, with unique non-empty registry identifiers. The dictionary name regicode is reserved for labels.

Data frames and named lists can also define mappings. A data frame needs a regicode column and a column matching attr:

mapping <- data.frame(
  regicode = c("410103", "410307", "411721"),
  custom = c("A", "A", "B"),
  hdi = c("high", "high", "low")
)
cr_map(mapping, attr = c("custom", "hdi"))
ls_vars("reframe") # Includes custom and hdi from the active directory
grouped <- cr_reframe(canregs, strat = "custom")
cr_map(list("410307" = "910000"), attr = "area_type")

With several names in attr, each selected column is stored separately and cr_map() returns a named list of effective dictionaries. Unselected columns are ignored. All selected inputs and target files are checked under writer locks before updates begin. An R-level write error restores previous files and removes new files; this is not a crash-safe multi-file transaction, and readers may see intermediate states during replacement. cache_refresh = TRUE clears previous overrides for every selected attribute before applying the new values.

The older write_registry(x, dict = ...) interface remains supported. Built-in province, city, region, and regicode groupings are derived from the identifiers and cannot be set through cr_map().

New files store only user overrides, tagged with a schema version and dictionary type. Reads merge these with the defaults in the installed package, so newly added defaults appear after a package update. Built-in area_type exceptions now apply even before any local dictionary file is created (for example, the built-in mapping classifies 410307 as 920000). Older versions used digit-based inference until an area-type dictionary file existed, which could produce different urban/rural groupings. Use the public ls_dict() reader rather than depending on the internal RDS layout. Reading a dictionary does not create or change a file.

Existing vector and label-table files remain readable. On their next successful update, a copy is retained alongside the file as *_dict.rds.backup-*, and the file is migrated. All legacy entries are retained as overrides: the old format cannot distinguish user edits from copied defaults. As a result, legacy entries can still mask changed defaults until explicitly reset. Backup files are omitted from ls_dict_files() and are not automatically deleted.

To restore current defaults, use reset_dict("registry") or reset_dict("regicode"). These operations back up an existing dictionary first. The older cache_refresh = TRUE option still resets overrides before applying the supplied update. Corrupt or incompatible files stop reads and updates, including reset, and remain untouched for inspection or recovery. After moving a damaged file aside, a new dictionary can be created normally.

Writes are verified in a temporary file before replacing the original. A writer lock prevents simultaneous updates or deletion; a conflicting operation reports an error rather than silently losing changes. If a process is terminated while holding a lock, verify that no writer is active before removing its *_dict.rds.lock directory and retrying. All dictionary operations respect the same canregtools.dict_dir setting.

Reproducibility notes

For reproducible registry analyses, record the following with the output:

  • the source files or data-frame preparation code;
  • the registry identifiers and the canreg construction method;
  • age_breaks, cancer_type, and any label_tail used by count_canreg();
  • the standard population and options used for rate estimation; and
  • any exclusions, denominator changes, or external comparison references.

This makes it possible to move from a published rate or quality indicator back to the source registry records and the exact fbswicd object used to calculate it.
